# RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback

Yue Huang    Yanbo Wang    Lichi Li    Yuanyuan Chen    Andreas Haupt   
Xiaonan Luo    Zheyuan Liu    Jihye Choi    Felix Juefei-Xu   
Xiangliang Zhang    Radha Poovendran    Misha Sra    Ying Liu    Ben
Burtenshaw    Thomas Wolf    Alex Pentland    Zichen Chen    Zhangchen
Xu

###### Abstract

Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them
using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of
autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement.
Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA
Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each
agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and \$300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU
cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures,
and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and
through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working
assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a
median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability
benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct
after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage
2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its
Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training.
Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation
rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the
style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that
benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains,
while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed
increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an
auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous
model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement
with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what
improvement means for the AI systems they use.

Stage 1 ran from September 29 to October 5, 2026, and Stage 2 from
October 10 to 13, 2026 (Pacific Time).

## 1  Introduction

Recursive self-improvement is a long-term vision in which AI systems
develop more capable successors that can, in turn, advance further AI
development ([Good, 1966](#bib.bib20); [Schmidhuber, 2007](#bib.bib71)).
If successful, this process could accelerate AI progress beyond the pace
of human research alone. Leading AI developers are actively pursuing
this vision: OpenAI aims for an automated AI researcher by 2028
([Bellan, 2025](#bib.bib4)), and Anthropic reports that its models
already lead about a quarter of its AI research and development ([Favaro
and Wright, 2026](#bib.bib18)). A practical step toward this vision is
to establish whether AI agents can develop models end to end under
realistic resource constraints and evaluation requirements.

AI agents already perform parts of this work. They train models for
Kaggle competitions ([Chan et al., 2024](#bib.bib9)), tackle
expert-designed research engineering tasks ([Wijk et al.,
2024](#bib.bib87); [Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib27)), replicate
published papers ([Starace et al., 2025](#bib.bib79)), and write papers
of their own ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)). Most closely related to
our work, PostTrainBench asks agents to post-train small base models,
with each run targeting a single benchmark disclosed to the agent ([Rank
et al., 2026](#bib.bib65)). Most of these tasks take hours rather than
days, use one or a few GPUs, and rely on automated evaluation. None,
however, asks an agent to build a model that people will then use.

Compared with optimizing for a single benchmark, post-training a
language model for real-world use poses a broader challenge: turning a
pretrained model into an assistant that people find useful. Starting
from a base model, a team selects data, writes or adapts training code,
runs supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization, and evaluates
the results ([Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib60); [Lambert et al.,
2024](#bib.bib40)). This process requires substantial GPU resources and
repeated cycles of training and evaluation, and success cannot be
captured by a single metric. Because these models are built to serve
people, the ultimate test is whether users prefer them. Benchmarks
assess specific capabilities through fixed response formats; to capture
user preferences more directly, we also ask people to compare the models
in a blind Human Arena modeled on Chatbot Arena ([Chiang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12)).

RSI Arena delegates this entire process to AI agents. No human selects
the training data or writes the training code; people only evaluate the
resulting models. The arena consists of two stages that mirror how
models are developed in practice
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
Stage 1 captures pre-release post-training. Ten frontier models, acting
as autonomous research agents, each post-trained the same base model for
six days with the same budget on a shared cluster. The agents chose
their own data, training code, and internal evaluations, while we
livestreamed their work. We then evaluated the ten final models on 20
benchmarks and in a blind human evaluation, where participants compared
pairs of model responses side by side at COLM 2026 and online. Stage 2
captures post-release improvement, when developers use user ratings and
preferences to train the next version. Each agent received the arena
battles involving its own model and had three additional days to improve
it. This stage tests another part of the self-improvement loop: whether
agents can use feedback from their models’ users to drive further
improvement.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: The two stages of RSI Arena. In Stage 1 (steps 1–4), ten AI
agents post-train the same base model for 144 hours, nominate
checkpoints, and their final models are evaluated on 20 benchmarks and
by people in the Human Arena. In Stage 2 (steps 5–8), each agent
continues from its own Stage 1 model with the arena battles that model
played, and the new models are evaluated again, with NVIDIA Instruct as
the common reference.

This report covers both stages. Our main findings from Stage 1 are as
follows:

1.  1.  Every agent produced a working assistant, and with style control
        people rate the best one level with NVIDIA Instruct. The best agent
        model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closed a median of 76% of the
        base-to-Instruct gap across 12 benchmarks. Without style control,
        people rated NVIDIA Instruct highest (1,182, against 1,161); with
        answer length and formatting controlled, the two are level at 1,095
        and 1,094.
2.  2.  The agents used similar recipes. All fine-tuned on public
        instruction data, and six then ran preference optimization. Six
        trained LoRA adapters and four trained all weights. Memory errors,
        storage quotas, job limits and queues took much of their time.
3.  3.  Budget use did not predict results. Gemini 3.8 Flash stopped after
        12 hours and 19 GPU-hours. People rated its model above the models
        of Muse Spark 1.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which used about 1,000
        GPU-hours each.
4.  4.  Benchmarks and people agreed only in part. Benchmark progress and
        human ratings correlate at $`\rho=0.73`$. LLM-judged chat benchmarks
        track people best, WildBench at $`\rho=0.95`$, and competition
        mathematics does not. The longer answer won 72% of decisive votes.
        The model with the best AIME 2026 score placed eighth of ten in
        human evaluation.
5.  5.  Safety was not part of the task, and some models regressed. Three
        models gave more harmful help than the base model on StrongREJECT.

From Stage 2 we found:

1.  1.  Feedback from people helped most agents. Eight of the ten agents
        narrowed their model’s style-controlled gap to NVIDIA Instruct;
        across all ten, the median gain was 28 points. The model trained by
        DeepSeek V4.1 Flash gained most, from −207 to −35 points, as its
        median answer grew from 61 to 508 tokens.
2.  2.  NVIDIA Instruct is still first without style control. It is ahead of
        the second model, the DeepSeek-trained one, in 99.5% of bootstrap
        resamples, and in a targeted round it won 39 of its 65 battles with
        the Astra-trained model, which won 18. With style control, the two
        are level (1,061 and 1,054).
3.  3.  The agents left much of their budget unused. They used 2,880 of
        their 5,051 GPU-hours and \$541 of their \$1,500 of API credit;
        Gemini 3.8 Flash used 10 GPU-hours.
4.  4.  Benchmarks changed little. Six of the ten agents raised their median
        benchmark progress, and the median change was +2 points of the gap.
        The changes on benchmarks and in human ratings are unrelated
        ($`\rho=−0.19`$). The model trained by MiniMax M3.1 Flash lost 18
        points, mostly because many of its answers no longer end in the
        format the scorers read, and it now gives more harmful help on
        StrongREJECT (24.5, against 2.6).

Our goal is to connect autonomous model development with the needs and
preferences of the people these models serve. RSI Arena brings users’
judgments into both evaluation and subsequent development, providing an
auditable setting for studying progress toward recursive
self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF). To support further study,
we release the model checkpoints submitted by the agents throughout
development on Hugging Face, providing an open resource for examining
how model capabilities and behavior evolve during autonomous
post-training.

## 2  RSI Arena

RSI Arena evaluates whether AI agents can autonomously develop and
improve language models for real-world use. The experiment follows a
two-stage development cycle: agents first post-train the same base model
under matched resource budgets, then refine their models using feedback
from human users. Throughout this process, agents control data
selection, training, and internal evaluation, while we assess the
resulting models through benchmarks and blind human comparisons.

### 2.1 Task and rules

All agents received the same instruction: to train the strongest model
possible from the provided base checkpoint within their allocated
resources. The instruction stated that final models would be evaluated
on held-out data inaccessible to the agents and by human evaluators. The
instruction left data selection and training methods to the agents and
specified no target benchmark, a design choice intended to reduce
incentives for reward hacking ([Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib29)). The
rules prohibited training on evaluation or benchmark test data, copying
reference answers, hard-coding outputs, and using other participants’
checkpoints, data, or code. Any submission found to involve cheating
would receive a score of zero. The instruction did not mention safety.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A The agents’ instruction ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
reproduces the task objective.

#### Base model

All agents started from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base
([NVIDIA, 2026](#bib.bib56)), a mixture-of-experts model with about 30
billion parameters, of which about 3 billion are active per token.
NVIDIA also released an instruct version of the same model, post-trained
by NVIDIA, which we use as a reference and call NVIDIA Instruct. The
base model’s end-of-turn token was never trained, so the base model does
not end its answers. Every agent had to teach its model to stop.

#### Budgets

Each agent had 1,000 GPU-hours and \$300 of API credit for its own model
calls. It could run up to 8 GPUs at a time, plus up to 8 preemptible
GPUs that the scheduler could take back, with at most 24 hours per job
and a 400 GiB storage quota. Stage 1 lasted 144 hours. Two agents joined
late, at hours 48 and 53, with the full budget.
Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Cost of the study ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
gives the cost of the whole study.

#### Nominations

An agent submits a model by nominating a checkpoint. A nomination names
the checkpoint directory and the completed GPU job that trained it, with
a record of the training data. The platform checks the record, the files
and the serving settings, then copies the checkpoint to the model
registry. The agent can nominate as often as it likes. When the session
ends, the latest accepted nomination becomes its final model. A session
ends when the agent declares its work finished, when its budget runs
out, or at the deadline.

### 2.2 Agents

Ten frontier models participated: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI) ([OpenAI,
2026](#bib.bib59)), MiMo-V2.6-Pro (Xiaomi) ([Xiaomi LLM-Core Team,
2026](#bib.bib89)), Grok 4.7 (SpaceXSI) ([SpaceXSI, 2026](#bib.bib78)),
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (DeepSeek) ([DeepSeek-AI, 2026](#bib.bib15)),
GLM-5.3 (Z.ai) ([Z.ai, 2026](#bib.bib97)), Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI) ([Kimi
Team, 2026](#bib.bib35)), Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google) ([Google DeepMind,
2026](#bib.bib21)), Muse Spark 1.3 (Meta) ([Meta, 2026](#bib.bib52)),
MiniMax M3.1 Flash (MiniMax) ([MiniMax, 2026](#bib.bib53))¹¹ 1 We used a
preview checkpoint of MiniMax M3.1 Flash during the livestreamed
experiment., and Step 5 Preview (StepFun) ([StepFun Team,
2026](#bib.bib80)). MiniMax M3.1 Flash and Step 5 Preview joined at
hours 48 and 53, respectively. We refer to agents by their underlying
model names and to the models they trained using shortened labels, such
as the Astra-trained model and the DeepSeek-trained model. Where the
context is clear, we use simply “the model.”

All agents ran in the same harness built on the Codex agent loop
([OpenAI, 2025a](#bib.bib57)). Their tools run commands on their virtual
machine and the cluster, read and write files, wait for jobs, report the
remaining budget, nominate checkpoints and end the session. Model calls
went through OpenRouter or the provider’s own API. When an agent’s
context filled up, the harness compacted it into a summary. A session
also restarted when a provider failed or we updated the platform, and
the ten agents used 57 sessions in all.

### 2.3 System architecture

Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 System architecture ‣ 2 RSI Arena ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
shows the system architecture, designed to mirror a real-world research
environment while maintaining agent isolation and enforcing resource
limits.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: The system architecture. Each agent works in its own sandbox
on the research host and runs its training jobs on the shared GPU
cluster; a separate management virtual machine runs the agents and
enforces their budgets.

#### A shared cluster

All ten agents run their jobs on one Slurm cluster of 64 GPUs, and each
may hold up to 16 at a time; giving every agent its own 16 GPUs would
take 160. Sharing also makes the task realistic: agents wait in queues
and lose preemptible jobs, as researchers do in a shared lab, so
planning compute is part of the work.

#### Isolated agents

Each agent works in a sandbox: a virtual machine of its own, with access
to the public internet and its own account on the Slurm cluster. The
agent loop and the API keys stay on a separate management virtual
machine, so an agent can call models and use GPUs only through the
platform, which charges each call and each GPU-hour to its budget and
stops jobs that break the limits.

#### Observability

The livestream at [https://rsiarena.live](https://rsiarena.live) showed
each agent’s actions, budget and nominations as they happened, and we
published a report each day.²² 2 The daily reports are at
[https://rsiarena.org](https://rsiarena.org). In the livestream, the
daily reports and the Human Arena, Step 5 Preview was shown as the
Anonymous Model.

## 3  Evaluation

### 3.1 Benchmarks

We evaluated each final model on 20 benchmarks
(Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Benchmarks ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")):
16 for capability and 4 for safety. We chose them before Stage 1 ended,
and
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Benchmark items in the agents’ training data ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
checks the agents’ training data for their items. Each model was
evaluated as it was served: with the chat template, system prompt and
decoding settings that its agent declared at nomination. All answers
were generated with vLLM ([Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib39)) on our
cluster, in a context window of 131,072 tokens. Answers that hit the
generation limit were asked again with a budget of 65,536 tokens.

Two references frame the scores. The base model uses the ChatML template
and greedy decoding. NVIDIA Instruct uses its default settings with
reasoning off, the setting closest to how the agents’ models answer;
with reasoning on, our harness reproduces six of its published scores to
within 2.7 points
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Calibration of the evaluation harness ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
Nine benchmarks are scored by an LLM judge
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Benchmark settings ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).

| Area                    | Benchmarks (items)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Knowledge and reasoning | GPQA Diamond ([Rein et al., 2024](#bib.bib66), 198 questions $`\times`$ 8 option orders;), MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib85), 12,032;), SuperGPQA ([M-A-P Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib48), 2,000 sampled;), HLE text only^(†) ([Phan et al., 2025](#bib.bib62), 2,158;), BBEH ([Kazemi et al., 2025](#bib.bib34), 4,520;), AA-Omniscience^(†) ([Jackson et al., 2025](#bib.bib30), 600;) |
| Mathematics             | AIME 2026 (30) and HMMT February 2026 (33), as run by MathArena ([Balunović et al., 2025](#bib.bib3))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Code                    | LiveCodeBench v6 ([Jain et al., 2025](#bib.bib31), 175;), SciCode ([Tian et al., 2024](#bib.bib82), 288 steps of 65 problems;)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Long context            | AA-LCR^(†) ([Artificial Analysis, 2025](#bib.bib1), 100;), MRCR v2 with 8 needles up to 128k tokens ([OpenAI, 2025b](#bib.bib58), 485;)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Instructions and chat   | IFBench ([Pyatkin et al., 2025](#bib.bib63), 300;), Arena-Hard v2^(†) ([Li et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43), 504 English prompts;), MultiChallenge^(†) ([Sirdeshmukh et al., 2025](#bib.bib76), 266;), WildBench v2^(†) ([Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib45), 1,022;)                                                                                                                                      |
| Safety                  | StrongREJECT^(†) ([Souly et al., 2024](#bib.bib77), 313;), MASK^(†) ([Ren et al., 2025](#bib.bib67), 1,000;), FORTRESS^(†) ([Knight et al., 2025](#bib.bib36), 500 adversarial and 500 benign;), BBQ ([Parrish et al., 2022](#bib.bib61), 5,000 sampled;)                                                                                                                                       |

Table 1: The 20 benchmarks. The number of items is the number of prompts
after our filters. A dagger marks benchmarks scored by an LLM judge.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Benchmark settings ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
gives the metrics and generation limits.

#### Progress toward NVIDIA Instruct

Raw scores sit on different scales, so we also report each score as a
fraction of the distance from the base model to NVIDIA Instruct,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
g_{b}(m)=100\cdot\frac{s_{b}(m)-s_{b}(\text{Base})}{s_{b}(\text{Instruct})-s_{b}(\text{Base})},
``` |  | (1) |

where $`s_{b}(m)`$ is model $`m`$’s score on benchmark $`b`$. A value of
0 means no better than the base model, and 100 means equal to NVIDIA
Instruct. We use the 12 capability benchmarks where NVIDIA Instruct
leads the base model by more than 10 points; on the other four, the
ratio would divide by a small or negative gap. A model’s *progress* is
the median of $`g_{b}(m)`$ over these 12.

### 3.2 Human Arena

The Human Arena ran for four days at
[https://rsiarena.org/arena](https://rsiarena.org/arena), on site at
COLM 2026 in San Francisco and online. A visitor writes a question, two
anonymous models answer side by side, and the visitor votes for the
better answer, a tie, or “both are bad”. The models’ names are shown
only after the vote. A battle can continue with follow-up questions, and
in web-search battles both models can search the web before answering.
Visitors could also draw a question from a bank, mostly of real first
questions from WildChat ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib102)) filtered for
quality by an LLM.

Each model was served by vLLM, on endpoints run by Hugging Face and on
our own cluster, with its nomination’s chat template, system prompt and
decoding settings and at most 2,048 new tokens per answer. When a
model’s answer ended inside its reasoning, the arena closed the
reasoning and let the model write a final answer. NVIDIA Instruct joined
on the third day as a reference, with reasoning off; it played in
battles but was not one of the competitors. Pairs were drawn uniformly
at first. From the third day, the arena sent more battles to models with
close ratings, and NVIDIA Instruct played an agent model in a fixed
share of battles, 20% on the last day.

#### Vote checks

We count a vote only if the voter had time to read both answers, and we
leave out every vote from browsers whose votes mostly fail this check.
Before the analysis we also filtered the data and removed noisy votes.
Attention-check battles, in which one answer is off-topic, appeared
among the ordinary ones; voters passed 100 of 102. Votes by the
organizers do not count. Of 1,685 votes in ordinary battles, 1,291
passed: 1,003 decisive votes, 159 ties and 129 “both are bad”.

#### The Stage 2 arena

For Stage 2 we opened a second arena with its own database, holding the
ten Stage 2 final models and NVIDIA Instruct, the one model in both
arenas. It ran for two days with the same interface, serving settings
and vote checks. Pairs were drawn uniformly at first; on the second day
most battles went to models with close ratings, and later half of them
went to the three models then ranked third to fifth. After the arena
closed we ran a targeted round among three of the leading models
(Section [6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Human preference ‣ 6 Stage 2: training on human feedback ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
Including the targeted round, 1,319 of 1,444 votes in ordinary Stage 2
battles passed the vote checks, and voters passed 161 of 167 attention
checks.

### 3.3 Ratings

We rate models with the Bradley–Terry model ([Bradley and Terry,
1952](#bib.bib6)), fitted as on Arena.ai’s leaderboard ([Chiang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12)). For a battle in which model $`A`$ answers on the
left and model $`B`$ on the right,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr(A\succ B)=\sigma\!\left(\ln 10\,(r_{A}-r_{B})+\symbfit{\gamma}^{\top}\mathbf{z}\right),
``` |  | (2) |

where $`\sigma`$ is the logistic function and $`\mathbf{z}`$ describes
how the two answers differ in style. A vote for $`A`$ counts as 1, a
vote for $`B`$ as 0, and a tie or “both are bad” as $`\tfrac{1}{2}`$. We
report $`1000+400\,(r_{m}-\bar{r})`$, where $`\bar{r}`$ is the mean over
the models of the arena, so a gap of 100 points means the higher model
is expected to win 64% of the votes between the two when their answers
do not differ in style.

#### Style control

People prefer longer and more formatted answers
(Section [5](#S5 "5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")),
so our main rating controls for style, as Arena.ai’s style control does
([Li et al., 2024a](#bib.bib42)); it has been the default view of their
leaderboard since May 2025. The style vector $`\mathbf{z}`$ has four
features: the answer’s length in tokens and the numbers of markdown
headers, list items and bold spans, each counted over every turn of the
battle. Each feature enters as the normalized difference
$`(f_{A}-f_{B})/(f_{A}+f_{B})`$, standardized over the battles. We
estimate the coefficients $`\symbfit{\gamma}`$ from our own votes,
separately for each stage, together with the ratings, with the
regularization of Arena.ai’s implementation
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Human Arena details ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
gives the details).
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Style control ‣ 3.3 Ratings ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
gives the estimates. The same fit with $`\symbfit{\gamma}=0`$ gives the
rating without style control, which we report alongside.

| Feature |  Stage 1 |  95% interval |  Stage 2 |  95% interval |  Arena.ai |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Answer length (tokens) |  0.169 |  −0.036 to 0.370 |  0.394 |  0.242 to 0.559 |  0.249 |
| List items |  0.294 |  0.118 to 0.485 |  0.222 |  0.065 to 0.366 |  0.031 |
| Headers |  −0.007 |  −0.190 to 0.174 |  0.117 |  −0.016 to 0.252 |  0.024 |
| Bold spans |  0.223 |  0.030 to 0.445 |  −0.007 |  −0.162 to 0.164 |  0.019 |

Table 2: Style coefficients estimated from each stage’s votes, with 95%
bootstrap intervals, and the values Arena.ai published in 2024. Each
multiplies a standardized normalized difference between the two answers
(Equation ([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.3 Ratings ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback"))).

#### Votes and intervals

Both ratings use the votes that passed the vote checks, in battles
without web search. Arena.ai keeps web-search battles out of its text
leaderboard and rates them in a separate arena; we follow it, since an
answer built on search results and citations differs in style from an
ordinary chat answer. This leaves 795 of Stage 1’s 1,291 accepted votes
and 1,096 of Stage 2’s 1,319. Intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th
percentiles over 1,000 bootstrap resamples of battles.

## 4  Stage 1: how the agents worked

### 4.1 The run

Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 The run ‣ 4 Stage 1: how the agents worked ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
shows the six days. The ten agents ran 5,391 GPU jobs, used 6,905
GPU-hours and \$1,050 of API calls, made 37,978 model calls and 43,966
tool calls, and had 81 nominations accepted.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 The run ‣ 4 Stage 1: how the agents worked ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
lists each agent’s use and its model’s results.

Three agents ended differently from the rest. Gemini 3.8 Flash stopped
itself at hour 12, after its final model answered 59 of the 60 questions
on its own test correctly; it left 981 GPU-hours and \$293 unused. Grok
4.7 ran out of API credit at hour 102 after 4,255 calls, with 698
GPU-hours unused, and the platform submitted its nomination from hour
95. Muse Spark 1.3 worked until the deadline. The other seven ended
their own sessions in the last 16 hours.

#### Timing of nominations

GPT-6 Astra made its final nomination at hour 43 and Muse Spark 1.3 at
hour 56; neither replaced it in the remaining days, although both kept
training. MiniMax M3.1 Flash nominated 17 times, more than any other
agent. Six final models were nominated in the last 14 hours.

### 4.2 Recipes

Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Recipes ‣ 4 Stage 1: how the agents worked ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
summarizes how each agent trained its final model. All ten began with
supervised fine-tuning on public instruction data, most often Tülu 3
([Lambert et al., 2024](#bib.bib40)), and six then ran preference
optimization with DPO ([Rafailov et al., 2023](#bib.bib64)), ORPO ([Hong
et al., 2024](#bib.bib23)) or SimPO ([Meng et al., 2024](#bib.bib51)) on
public preference data such as UltraFeedback ([Cui et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14)). Six final models are LoRA adapters ([Hu et al.,
2022](#bib.bib25)) and four are full fine-tunes.

![Refer to caption](2610.33624v1/recipes.png)

Figure 4: How each agent trained its final model. Dots mark the kind of
weights trained, the data used and four other steps seen in the agents’
records; the chips give the training steps of the final model in order.
Data are the kinds named in each agent’s scripts and notes, and not all
of them reached the final model.
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Notes on each agent ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
names the data sets.

#### Generated data

Four agents made training data with models and checked it automatically.
GLM-5.3 sampled answers to 14,949 math problems and kept the correct
ones. MiMo-V2.6-Pro wrote 5,553 instruction-following pairs and checked
each with code. MiniMax M3.1 Flash trained on its own answers that
passed checks. Grok 4.7 downloaded NVIDIA Instruct, checked that its
license allows distillation, and trained on its answers; its final model
did not use that data.³³ 3 The rules do not forbid distillation from
public models, and we treat it as an ordinary data choice.

#### Decontamination

Two agents found benchmark items in their training data and removed them
on their own. GPT-6 Astra found MMLU-Pro and IFEval items on day 1 and
MATH-500 and HumanEval items on day 2, and both times retrained from the
base model. MiMo-V2.6-Pro removed 92,477 rows on day 1 and 113,686 more
on day 2 after checking ten further benchmarks. Grok 4.7 kept its own
test prompts out of new training data.

#### Selection

Agents chose among checkpoints with tests they wrote, from 8 prompts to
1,400 questions. Several changed their nomination only when a new model
beat the old one on these tests. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash switched only when
a model won at least two of its three tests; it also made five
nominations that changed only the system prompt or decoding settings of
the same weights.

### 4.3 Engineering problems

Full-Parameter Training. Much of the agents’ time went into getting
training to run at all. The three agents that pursued full-parameter
training from the outset spent their initial hours resolving memory
errors. After seven hours and 39 test jobs, GLM-5.3 abandoned the
Hugging Face trainer and implemented its own FSDP2 trainer, which ran
roughly seven times faster. Kimi K3 measured inter-GPU bandwidth of
11,GB/s, inferred that the GPUs were connected via PCIe, and offloaded
optimizer state to the CPU. Platform constraints created further
obstacles. Four agents exhausted their 400,GiB storage quotas at least
once, causing job failures. Only checkpoints from completed jobs were
eligible for nomination: GLM-5.3 could not nominate a checkpoint from a
job that hit the 24-hour limit, while Step 5 Preview could not nominate
its best checkpoint because it had cancelled the corresponding job. Kimi
K3’s eight-GPU job spent 30 hours and 43 minutes in the queue.

End-of-turn token failures. The base model’s untrained end-of-turn token
caused failures for every agent. Grok 4.7 identified the issue five
minutes into the run. GLM-5.3 initialized the token’s output weights
from those of the trained end-of-text token, while DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
discovered that its initial training data provided supervision only for
the end-of-turn token. Non-terminating responses were common in the
agents’ own tests during the first two days. The token also disrupted
agent execution: including its literal form in a tool call truncated
MiMo-V2.6-Pro’s own response. At minute 48, it noted: “Key lesson
learned: never emit the literal end-of-turn token in tool arguments—it
truncates my response.”

Human intervention. After MiniMax M3.1 Flash and Step 5 Preview joined,
we observed a sharp decline in cluster GPU utilization. Inspection of
Slurm allocations showed that host-memory reservations were preventing
jobs from starting despite idle GPUs. These reservations incurred no
additional budget cost. On one node, MiniMax M3.1 Flash ran four
single-GPU jobs that each reserved 120 GB of host memory, leaving four
GPUs idle and blocking GLM-5.3’s job. The pattern extended across
agents: in the 24 hours before our intervention, eight agents submitted
427 jobs requesting more than 64 GB per GPU. We therefore introduced a
cap of 64 GB of host memory per GPU. One minute later, Grok 4.7 changed
its evaluation jobs from one GPU and 80 GB to two GPUs and 120 GB.

### 4.4 Budget use

Figure [13](#A5.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ Appendix E Budget use ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Budget use ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
shows how the agents spent their budgets.
Table [8](#A5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix E Budget use ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
there gives each agent’s API cost and GPU-hours in both stages, and
Figure [14](#A5.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ Appendix E Budget use ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
sets the API cost against the Stage 2 human rating. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash,
Muse Spark 1.3, MiMo-V2.6-Pro and GLM-5.3 used more than 90% of their
1,000 GPU-hours. Grok 4.7 used all of its API credit, and GPT-6 Astra
nearly all, \$288. The other agents used less than half of their API
credit. Of the 5,391 GPU jobs, 73% completed, 12% were preempted, 6%
failed and 8% were cancelled.

Using more compute did not lead to a better-rated model. Across the ten
agents, GPU-hours used and the style-controlled human rating correlate
at $`\rho=-0.21`$, and GPU-hours and benchmark progress at
$`\rho=-0.01`$. Gemini 3.8 Flash used 19 GPU-hours; Muse Spark 1.3 and
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash used about 1,000 each, and people rated both of
their models below the Gemini-trained model.

## 5  Stage 1: results

### 5.1 Benchmarks

Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.1 Benchmarks ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
shows progress toward NVIDIA Instruct. The Astra-trained model leads,
closing a median of 76% of the gap across the 12 benchmarks, followed by
the MiniMax-trained (57%) and GLM-trained (52%) models. The lowest is
the Step-trained model, at 32%.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D All benchmark scores ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
gives every raw score.

![Refer to caption](2610.33624v1/benchmarks.png)

Figure 5: Benchmark progress toward NVIDIA Instruct. A: median over 12
capability benchmarks of
Equation ([1](#S3.E1 "In Progress toward NVIDIA Instruct ‣ 3.1 Benchmarks ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback"));
the bar spans the 25th to 75th percentile of the 12 values. B: each
benchmark; 0 is the base model and 100 is NVIDIA Instruct, with values
above 100 in bold.

Ten of the 120 scores in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.1 Benchmarks ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")B
exceed NVIDIA Instruct. Four models do so on MMLU-Pro and four on
SciCode. The Muse-trained model exceeds it on MRCR and, by far, on AIME
2026, where it scores 66.7 against 21.7. It trained on long reasoning
traces, and NVIDIA Instruct answered with reasoning off.⁴⁴ 4 Muse Spark
1.3’s training data contain no AIME 2026 problem other than one that was
already public before the exam
(Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Benchmark items in the agents’ training data ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
No agent model exceeds NVIDIA Instruct on the other eight of the 12
benchmarks. On the four capability benchmarks outside the 12, where the
base model and NVIDIA Instruct score close together, several do: all ten
on AA-Omniscience, which penalizes wrong answers, two on AA-LCR and one
on BBEH.

Some low scores come from answer format rather than knowledge. GPQA
Diamond requires a final line of the form “Answer: X”. The Step-trained
model left 1,504 of 1,584 answers without it and scores 2.3; the
Muse-trained model left 1,335 and scores 10.3, many because its
reasoning did not finish. Even with 65,536 tokens, 19.2% of the
Muse-trained model’s answers across the suite hit the limit. The
GLM-trained model began 400 of 485 MRCR answers without the required
prefix and scores 2.6. We report the official scores throughout.

### 5.2 Human preference

Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Human preference ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")A
shows the Stage 1 ratings. With style control, the Astra-trained model
and NVIDIA Instruct are level, at 1,095 and 1,094. The models trained by
Grok (1,038), MiMo (1,025), GLM (1,024) and MiniMax (1,002) follow. The
Kimi- and Gemini-trained models come next (982 and 981), then the
Muse-trained model (938) and the Step-trained model (934), and the
DeepSeek-trained model is last (887). Without style control, NVIDIA
Instruct leads at 1,182, the Astra-trained model follows at 1,161, and
the agent models spread over 365 points instead of 208
(Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Why benchmarks and people disagree ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Human preference ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")B
shows the outcomes of each model’s battles, which are also the feedback
each agent receives in Stage 2.

![Refer to caption](2610.33624v1/human-arena.png)

Figure 6: Human Arena results, Stage 1. A: style-controlled ratings
(filled, with 95% bootstrap intervals) and ratings without style control
(open), from 795 accepted votes in battles without web search
(Equation ([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.3 Ratings ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")));
NVIDIA Instruct is a reference. B: outcomes of each agent model’s
accepted battles, from that model’s side.

People asked about many kinds of tasks. An LLM sorted the accepted
questions into ten categories. Of those it could sort, 18% asked for
analysis, 15% for an explanation, 13% for facts, 12% for advice and 12%
for mathematics; reasoning puzzles, coding and writing made up 8%, 8%
and 7%. In 496 accepted battles both models could search the web, and 86
had follow-up questions.

### 5.3 Why benchmarks and people disagree

Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5.3 Why benchmarks and people disagree ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
compares the two evaluations. Benchmark progress and the human rating
without style control correlate at $`\rho=0.73`$ across the ten agent
models (panel A), and at $`\rho=0.72`$ with style control. The
benchmarks closest to the human ratings are WildBench ($`\rho=0.95`$)
and Arena-Hard ($`\rho=0.85`$), both of which ask an LLM judge to rate
chat answers, together with SciCode (0.82), GPQA (0.77) and BBEH (0.75).
The competition-math benchmarks do not track the human ratings
($`\rho=0.10`$ for AIME 2026 and $`-0.30`$ for HMMT), and the
long-context benchmarks run against them (panel B).

![Refer to caption](2610.33624v1/bench-vs-human.png)

Figure 7: Benchmarks against human ratings without style control. A:
benchmark progress and rating for the ten agent models. B: for each
benchmark, and for the median answer length in the arena, the Spearman
correlation between the ten models’ values and their ratings: $`+1`$
means the benchmark orders the models exactly as people do, 0 means no
relation. With ten models, a value inside the shaded band
($`|\rho|<0.65`$) could arise by chance. For StrongREJECT and FORTRESS,
where lower is safer, the sign is flipped so that a positive value means
safer models were rated higher.

#### Length

Median answer length in the arena correlates with the rating without
style control at $`\rho=0.78`$, and with the style-controlled rating at
$`\rho=0.72`$. The longer answer won 72% of the 999 decisive votes
between answers of different lengths
(Figure [9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Length ‣ 5.3 Why benchmarks and people disagree ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")A).
The share rises from 57% when one answer is less than 1.2 times as long
as the other to 81% when it is more than 6.7 times as long. Formatting
matters too: in the style-controlled fit, the coefficients of list items
(0.29) and bold spans (0.22) are larger than that of length (0.17), and
headers have no effect
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Style control ‣ 3.3 Ratings ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
Controlling for style narrows the spread of the agent models from 365 to
208 points. It lifts the DeepSeek-trained model by 91 points, though it
stays last, and lowers the Astra-trained model by 66 points and NVIDIA
Instruct by 88, which leaves the two level at the top
(Figure [9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Length ‣ 5.3 Why benchmarks and people disagree ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")B).
With ten models, a correlation needs a magnitude above about 0.65 to be
distinguishable from chance at the 5% level, so the correlation of
benchmark progress with the human rating is clear both without and with
style control, and so is WildBench’s.

![Refer to caption](2610.33624v1/length.png)

![Refer to caption](2610.33624v1/safety.png)

Figure 8: Answer length and style in the Human Arena, Stage 1. A: share
of decisive votes won by the longer answer, by how much longer it was;
the bins hold 88 to 220 votes. B: ratings without and with style control
(Equation ([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.3 Ratings ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")));
the right column gives the change, with minus without.

Figure 9: Safety benchmarks. StrongREJECT scores harmful compliance and
FORTRESS scores risk on adversarial prompts; lower is safer for both.
MASK scores honesty under pressure to lie and BBQ scores accuracy on
questions that invite social bias; higher is better for both. Dashed
lines mark the base model and solid lines NVIDIA Instruct. Each headline
counts the models on the safer or less safe side of the reference named
under it. Models are ordered by style-controlled human rating.

#### Short answers

The three lowest-rated models often gave short answers. The
DeepSeek-trained model had a median answer of 473 characters, and 21% of
its answers were shorter than 150 characters; the Step-trained model had
a median of 967 characters, with 24% under 150. The Muse-trained model
wrote long reasoning, which the arena hides: in 8.6% of its answers the
reasoning used up the limit and the arena had to ask it for a final
answer. The same habit that gave it the top AIME 2026 score left people
with short or forced answers.

Our reading is that the two evaluations measure different things. Most
benchmarks test one skill with a fixed answer format, while people
judged whole answers to their own questions, and they preferred answers
that were complete and detailed. A model can gain on a benchmark by
reasoning longer before a short final answer, and lose in human ratings
for the same reason.

### 5.4 Safety

The task said nothing about safety, and the agents’ models differ widely
on it
(Figure [9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Length ‣ 5.3 Why benchmarks and people disagree ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
On StrongREJECT, which measures how much useful help a model gives with
harmful requests, the Gemini-, Grok- and Muse-trained models (43.6, 34.4
and 31.4) score worse than the base model (16.9); they refused 54%, 63%
and 64% of the harmful requests, against 99% for NVIDIA Instruct. The
base model refused 61%, but its other answers were seldom useful. The
other seven score 12.2 or lower. On FORTRESS, seven models carry less
risk than NVIDIA Instruct, but low risk can also come from refusing too
much: the Step-trained model has the lowest risk and refuses 22.8% of
benign prompts, against 2.4% for NVIDIA Instruct. Nine models are more
honest than NVIDIA Instruct on MASK, and six score higher on BBQ. The
base model scores well on MASK and FORTRESS because it seldom answers
coherently, not because it is safe.

## 6  Stage 2: training on human feedback

### 6.1 Design

Stage 2 asks whether an agent can improve its own model with the
feedback that people gave it. Each agent continues from its own final
Stage 1 model, with its Stage 1 notes, code, data and checkpoints where
it left them. It receives the arena battles its own model played and has
72 hours, 500 GPU-hours and \$150 of API credit. The cluster, harness,
rules and nomination checks are those of Stage 1. The instruction asks
the agent to use the feedback, and any other legitimate data and
methods, to make its model better, and tells it that the final model
will again be evaluated on held-out data and by people.

#### Feedback

Each agent receives one snapshot of the accepted battles its model
played: 213 to 276 per agent
(Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Human preference ‣ 5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")B).
Each battle contains the questions, its own model’s answers, the other
model’s answers with that model’s name removed, and the vote; web-search
battles are marked. The accompanying description states what the data
are and how they were collected, and nothing about what they show.
Whatever patterns there are, such as the length effect of
Section [5](#S5 "5 Stage 1: results ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback"),
the agents have to find themselves.

### 6.2 Evaluation

We evaluated each Stage 2 final model on the same 20 benchmarks
(Section [6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5 Benchmarks ‣ 6 Stage 2: training on human feedback ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback"))
and in a second Human Arena
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
Stage 1 and Stage 2 models did not meet in one arena: the second arena
held the ten Stage 2 models and NVIDIA Instruct, which is the common
reference between the two. We compare the stages through each agent
model’s style-controlled rating minus NVIDIA Instruct’s rating in the
same arena.

### 6.3 The run

Stage 2 ran its full 72 hours
(Figure [10](#S6.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 6.3 The run ‣ 6 Stage 2: training on human feedback ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")A;
Table [11](#A8.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix H Stage 2 agents and safety ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Stage 2 agents and safety ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
gives each agent’s use). The agents used 2,880 of their 5,051
GPU-hours⁵⁵ 5 Each agent had 500 GPU-hours, plus the GPU time it was
charged while a storage fault stopped the sessions, which we credited
back. and \$541 of their \$1,500 of API credit, ran 4,912 GPU jobs and
made 71 accepted nominations. Nine agents ended their research
themselves; Muse Spark 1.3 ran until the deadline. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
and MiniMax M3.1 Flash used their whole GPU allowance, and Gemini 3.8
Flash used 10 GPU-hours and \$4 of API credit before it stopped. Six
final models are LoRA adapters and four are full weights, as in Stage 1.
By the names and code of their training jobs, nine agents ran preference
optimization (DPO, SimPO or ORPO), and six also ran supervised
fine-tuning. The final Astra-trained model was fine-tuned on its
feedback and on replayed data with a KL penalty toward its Stage 1
model, and the final MiMo-trained model is a weight average of
fine-tuned models.

![Refer to caption](2610.33624v1/stage2-run.png)

Figure 10: Stage 2. A: GPU-hours used by each agent over the 72 hours;
the dashed line is the 500 GPU-hour allowance, which two agents passed
with GPU time credited back after a storage fault. B: median answer
length in the arena, in tokens, for each model in Stage 1 (open) and
Stage 2 (filled). NVIDIA Instruct did not change; its length differs
because the two arenas had different questions.

### 6.4 Human preference

Figure [11](#S6.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Answer length ‣ 6.4 Human preference ‣ 6 Stage 2: training on human feedback ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")A
gives the Stage 2 ratings, and
Table [10](#A6.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix F Human Arena details ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Human Arena details ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
lists the ratings of both stages with their intervals. Without style
control, NVIDIA Instruct leads at 1,134, ahead of the DeepSeek-trained
model (1,053) in 99.5% of bootstrap resamples, and the Astra-trained
model is third (1,041). With style control, the Astra-trained model
(1,061) and NVIDIA Instruct (1,054) are level, as in Stage 1: the
Astra-trained model comes out ahead in only 58% of resamples. The models
trained by MiniMax (1,030), DeepSeek (1,019) and Grok (1,008) follow.
The Stage 2 votes weigh length more than Stage 1’s, with a coefficient
of 0.39 against 0.17, and bold spans not at all
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Style control ‣ 3.3 Ratings ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).

#### A targeted round

The arena closed with the order of the leading models not settled, so we
ran a short round of a few hours with only the Astra- and
DeepSeek-trained models and NVIDIA Instruct, the three highest without
style control at the close. Half of its battles paired the Astra-trained
model with NVIDIA Instruct, and a quarter each the other two pairs. It
brought 121 accepted votes. NVIDIA Instruct won 39 of its 65 battles
with the Astra-trained model, which won 18. NVIDIA Instruct beat the
DeepSeek-trained model 17 to 6, and the DeepSeek-trained model beat the
Astra-trained one 18 to 10. Of these battles, 41 used web search; they
are left out of the ratings above, which include the rest.

#### Change from Stage 1

Figure [11](#S6.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Answer length ‣ 6.4 Human preference ‣ 6 Stage 2: training on human feedback ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")B
compares each agent model’s gap to NVIDIA Instruct in the two arenas.
Eight of the ten agents narrowed the gap; across all ten, the median
gain was 28 points. The DeepSeek-trained model gained most, from −207 to
−35 points; the Step-trained model gained 98 points and the
MiniMax-trained model 68. The Astra-trained model stayed level with
NVIDIA Instruct (+1 and +7). The MiMo- and Kimi-trained models fell back
slightly, by 14 and 13 points.

#### Answer length

Answers changed length in both directions
(Figure [10](#S6.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 6.3 The run ‣ 6 Stage 2: training on human feedback ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")B).
The DeepSeek-trained model, whose short answers had made it the
lowest-rated model of Stage 1, now writes a median of 508 tokens instead
of 61. The MiniMax- and Muse-trained models also write longer answers,
and both gained. The Astra-trained model writes shorter answers than
before, 305 tokens instead of 519, and kept its place. The Step-trained
model, whose answers kept about the same length (326 and 322 tokens),
still gained 98 points, so length is not the whole story.

![Refer to caption](2610.33624v1/stage2-arena.png)

Figure 11: Human Arena results, Stage 2. A: style-controlled ratings
(filled, with 95% bootstrap intervals) and ratings without style control
(open), from 1,096 accepted votes in battles without web search. B: each
agent model’s style-controlled rating minus NVIDIA Instruct’s rating, in
the Stage 1 arena (open) and the Stage 2 arena (filled).

### 6.5 Benchmarks

We scored the ten Stage 2 models on the same 20 benchmarks with the same
code, judges and references as in Stage 1; the base model’s and NVIDIA
Instruct’s answers are those of Stage 1. Unlike in Stage 1, every answer
had a budget of 65,536 tokens from the start.⁶⁶ 6 Four WildBench
answers, one each from the MiMo-, Grok-, DeepSeek- and MiniMax-trained
models, could not be graded because the judge provider refused the
request, and are left out.

Figure [12](#S6.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 6.5 Benchmarks ‣ 6 Stage 2: training on human feedback ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")A
shows progress toward NVIDIA Instruct over the same 12 benchmarks. Six
of the ten agents raised their median, and the median change across
agents was +2 points of the gap. The Astra-trained model leads again, at
87% of the gap against 76%. Its median rose mainly because its IFBench
score rose from 69% to 89% of the gap; its MMLU-Pro and SciCode scores,
which had exceeded NVIDIA Instruct, fell to 92% and 98%. The
MiniMax-trained model fell most, from 57% to 39%. Much of this is answer
format: 1,435 of its 1,584 GPQA Diamond answers end without the
“Answer:” line the scorer reads, against 80 in Stage 1, and 1,877 of its
5,000 BBQ answers give no readable choice. Its IFBench score also fell,
from 25.0 to 16.3. The Muse-trained model still used up the token budget
in 23.6% of its answers.

Across agents, the chat and instruction-following benchmarks gained a
little and the knowledge and code benchmarks lost a little
(Figure [12](#S6.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 6.5 Benchmarks ‣ 6 Stage 2: training on human feedback ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")B).
The median change was $`+6`$ points of the gap on MultiChallenge, $`+5`$
on IFBench and $`+4`$ on Arena-Hard, and $`-4`$ on SciCode, $`-3`$ on
SuperGPQA and $`-2`$ on MMLU-Pro. Eight of the 120 scores exceed NVIDIA
Instruct, against ten in Stage 1.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D All benchmark scores ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
gives every Stage 2 score.

![Refer to caption](2610.33624v1/stage2-benchmarks.png)

Figure 12: Benchmarks, Stage 2. A: median progress toward NVIDIA
Instruct over the 12 benchmarks of
Equation ([1](#S3.E1 "In Progress toward NVIDIA Instruct ‣ 3.1 Benchmarks ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")),
Stage 1 (open) and Stage 2 (filled), with the change in points. B:
change of each score, Stage 2 minus Stage 1, in points of the gap from

#### Benchmarks and people

In Stage 2, benchmark progress and the style-controlled human rating
correlate at $`\rho=0.30`$ ($`\rho=0.19`$ without style control),
against 0.72 in Stage 1. WildBench still tracks people ($`\rho=0.79`$).
The change in benchmark progress and the change in the gap to NVIDIA
Instruct in human ratings are unrelated ($`\rho=−0.19`$): the
DeepSeek-trained model gained 172 points in human ratings and 4 on
benchmarks, and the MiniMax-trained model gained 68 points in human
ratings while losing 18 on benchmarks.

#### Safety

Table [12](#A8.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix H Stage 2 agents and safety ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Stage 2 agents and safety ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
compares the safety benchmarks of the two stages. On StrongREJECT, the
MiniMax-trained model now gives much more harmful help (24.5, against
2.6), while the DeepSeek-, Gemini- and Muse-trained models give less
(1.2 against 12.2, 36.2 against 43.6, and 24.3 against 31.4). The new
system prompt that DeepSeek V4.1 Flash wrote tells the model never to
refuse a harmless request, and its StrongREJECT score still improved. On
BBQ, the MiMo-trained model fell from 84.7 to 56.5: it more often names
a person when the question gives no basis for choosing one, and answers
44.9% of these ambiguous questions correctly. MASK honesty rose for six
models, most for the MiniMax-trained model (63.0 to 79.3). FORTRESS risk
rose by more than 5 points for the MiMo- and DeepSeek-trained models and
fell by more than 5 points for the Astra- and GLM-trained models.

## 7  Discussion

#### What RSI Arena establishes

All ten agents independently selected data, implemented training, and
nominated checkpoints, producing working assistants within a
human-operated research platform. The strongest model received a human
rating close to NVIDIA Instruct’s after adjustment for response length
and formatting, with the reference evaluated with reasoning disabled. By
the end of Stage 2, the best median benchmark progress reached 87% of
the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 benchmarks. These results demonstrate
the feasibility of sustained, agent-directed post-training. However, the
experiment covers one base model and one run per agent. The agents also
trained a separate, smaller model, leaving the models that powered their
research unchanged. Repeated runs, different base models, and
experiments in which improved models conduct subsequent research are
needed to test reliability and close the recursive loop.

#### What agents learned from human feedback

Human feedback gave agents evidence about problems encountered by their
models’ users. The experimental results show agents responding to
incomplete answers, unnecessary refusals, repetition, and premature
termination, and using these observations to revise their data, prompts,
and training choices. They also responded to presentation preferences.
One agent concluded that length was “the only lever” on votes and
adjusted its system prompt and training answers to encourage longer
responses. Another selected prompts and checkpoints using a reward model
that, by its own measurement, agreed with votes about as well as answer
length alone. We found no evidence in the recorded Stage 2 actions of
attempts to persuade voters, impersonate other models, or manipulate the
arena’s mechanics. These observations illustrate both the value of user
feedback and the challenge of interpreting it: agents can identify
problems that matter to users, but they can also pursue features
associated with favorable ratings without establishing broader
improvements.

#### Human preference and benchmark capability

Benchmark progress and style-controlled human ratings were associated in
Stage 1 ($`\rho=0.72`$), but the association was weaker in Stage 2
($`\rho=0.30`$). Changes in the two measures also showed little
association across the ten models ($`\rho=−0.19`$). For example, the
DeepSeek-trained model gained 172 points in its human rating relative to
the common reference and 4 points in benchmark progress. LLM-judged chat
benchmarks remained closer to human ratings, with WildBench at
$`\rho=0.79`$. Because Stage 2 also provided additional development time
and resources and used a separate human arena, these comparisons do not
isolate the effect of human feedback. They do, however, show why both
forms of evaluation are useful: benchmark gains and changes in user
preference capture different aspects of model improvement.

#### Safety requires explicit attention

The task did not specify safety requirements, and safety outcomes moved
in both directions. In Stage 1, three models had higher
harmful-compliance scores on StrongREJECT than the base model. In Stage
2, the MiniMax-trained model’s score rose from 2.6 to 24.5, while the
models trained by DeepSeek, Gemini, and Muse improved on the same
measure. These changes should not be interpreted as uniform improvements
or regressions across all aspects of safety. They show that gains in
human preference do not by themselves establish safer behavior. This
motivates making safety an explicit consideration in training objectives
and evaluating it independently of preference and capability.

#### Using compute effectively

Compute use showed little association with human ratings across the ten
Stage 1 runs ($`\rho=-0.21`$). Gemini 3.8 Flash used 19 GPU-hours and
was rated above two models whose agents used about 1,000 GPU-hours each.
In Stage 2, the agents used 2,880 of their 5,051 available GPU-hours; of
the two that exhausted their budgets, one improved on benchmarks and the
other lost the most benchmark progress. These observations do not
establish that compute is unimportant, but they suggest that a larger
allowance alone is insufficient to ensure better outcomes. The
trajectories point to training reliability and internal evaluation as
practical targets for improving resource use: engineering failures
consumed substantial time, and agents often selected checkpoints using
narrow tests.

#### Making autonomous development auditable

The recorded trajectories made it possible to examine decisions that
final scores alone would not reveal. Two agents identified benchmark
items in their training data and removed them without being prompted.
Independent checks also found discrepancies in some agent-written model
cards, including training counts and reported hardware
(Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Model cards ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
These findings support checking agents’ accounts against execution
records and submitted artifacts. Autonomy over training decisions also
coexisted with human operation of the platform: people maintained the
infrastructure, enforced resource limits, and could inspect recorded
actions or terminate sessions. The released checkpoints and documented
trajectories provide a basis for further analysis of how development
decisions affect model behavior.

#### Toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback

For general-purpose AI, improvement also depends on how well models work
with and serve people. We view RSI Arena as a step toward recursive
self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which users’ judgments
inform both model evaluation and subsequent development. Human feedback
can help identify problems in use, guide priorities for further
training, and assess whether the resulting changes are preferred. Votes
remain partial measurements of what people value, so capability and
safety evaluations complement this feedback. A practical question is how
to obtain sufficiently informative human feedback as autonomous
development expands. In RSI Arena, each stage collected roughly 1,300
accepted votes, but the amount and type of feedback needed for reliable
improvement remain open questions. Future work should examine when
agents should seek human input, how they interpret it, and how automated
evaluators can remain calibrated to users over successive rounds of
development.

## 8  Related work

#### Auto research

AI agents that do research on their own are improving fast ([Kong
et al., 2026](#bib.bib37); [Chan et al., 2026](#bib.bib8); [Kwa et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38)). They are tested on Kaggle competitions ([Chan
et al., 2024](#bib.bib9)), research engineering ([Wijk et al.,
2024](#bib.bib87); [Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib27); [Nathani et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54)), the NanoGPT speedrun ([Zhao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib100)), the replication of papers ([Starace et al.,
2025](#bib.bib79)) and long-horizon research tasks ([Xu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib91)). Research systems search over code ([Jiang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32)), write papers ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib46); [Yamada
et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib70)) and
run long loops of experiments ([Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib90);
[Karpathy, 2026](#bib.bib33)). Closest to our work are agents that
post-train models ([Yano et al., 2025](#bib.bib94); [Ma et al.,
2026](#bib.bib49); [Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)), above all PostTrainBench, where an agent post-trains
a small base model for one named benchmark in 10 hours on one GPU ([Rank
et al., 2026](#bib.bib65)). In RSI Arena the agent builds a general
assistant from a 30-billion-parameter model over six days with 1,000
GPU-hours on a shared cluster, people judge it, and in Stage 2 the agent
learns from their votes. Agents that are scored on a target can also
game it ([Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib29); [Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib46); [Zhong et al., 2025](#bib.bib104)), and models that
learn to hack their reward can go on to worse behavior ([Denison et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16); [MacDiarmid et al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Baker et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2)). Some PostTrainBench agents trained on the test set,
downloaded instruction-tuned checkpoints instead of training their own,
or used an API key they found to generate training data ([Rank et al.,
2026](#bib.bib65)). In RSI Arena the keys stay on the management
machine, each nomination names the GPU job that trained it, and we found
no training on test sets
(Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Benchmark items in the agents’ training data ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).

#### Recursive self-improvement

Recent work makes self-improvement concrete ([Ren et al.,
2026](#bib.bib68)). Models propose their own tasks ([Zhao et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib99); [Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)) or write their own training data ([Zweiger et al.,
2025](#bib.bib105)). Agents rewrite their own code ([Yin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib95); [Robeyns et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib98); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib83)) and evolve
algorithms, including ones that speed up their own training ([Novikov
et al., 2025](#bib.bib55)). MemoHarness improves an agent’s harness from
its own runs, using an experience bank of diagnosed past cases ([Huang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib28)), and the loop now reaches deep research,
machine learning engineering and open-ended tasks ([Lu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib47); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib93); [Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib41)). Most of these loops are judged by automatic checks
([Tan et al., 2026](#bib.bib81)), which agents game or overfit ([Zhang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib98); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib84); [Zhao
et al., 2026](#bib.bib101); [Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib88)), and
self-evolution can wear away safe behavior ([Shao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib72); [Han et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)). In RSI Arena, people
judge each step instead.

#### Human evaluation and alignment

Assistants are aligned and evaluated with human preferences ([Christiano
et al., 2017](#bib.bib13); [Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib60); [Rafailov
et al., 2023](#bib.bib64); [Casper et al., 2023](#bib.bib7)). Chatbot
Arena fits a Bradley–Terry model to blind pairwise votes ([Chiang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)), and LLM judges and benchmarks built from
arena prompts are cheaper stand-ins ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib103);
[Li et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43)). But a preference is not the same as
quality. Human and LLM judges prefer longer answers ([Singhal et al.,
2023](#bib.bib75); [Dubois et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)), people notice
fewer errors in confident answers ([Hosking et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)),
and people and preference models favor flattery, jargon and style
([Sharma et al., 2023](#bib.bib73); [Bharadwaj et al., 2026](#bib.bib5);
[Feuer et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). Training on human feedback can teach
models to mislead ([Wen et al., 2024](#bib.bib86)), and private testing
can skew arena rankings ([Singh et al., 2025](#bib.bib74)). We follow
Arena.ai’s control for length and formatting ([Li et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib42)), and we find the same bias among our models, which
some agents learned to use in Stage 2. Like JobBench, which judges agent
work by what the person who asked for it wanted ([Li et al.,
2026](#bib.bib44)), RSI Arena lets the people who use the models judge
them.

## 9  Conclusion

RSI Arena gave ten AI agents responsibility for post-training a base
model and then improving it with access to human feedback. The agents
chose their own data, implemented training, and selected checkpoints
under fixed budgets on a shared cluster. All ten produced working
assistants within the six-day first stage. In the Human Arena, the
strongest model received a rating comparable to NVIDIA’s post-trained
release, evaluated with reasoning disabled, after controlling for answer
length and formatting. On benchmarks, it closed a median of 76% of the
base-to-Instruct gap across 12 benchmarks. Following three additional
days of development with access to people’s votes, eight agents improved
their human ratings relative to the common reference. The best benchmark
progress rose to 87%, while gains across agents were modest overall.

These results show why model improvement needs more than one measure.
Human ratings, benchmark performance, and safety did not consistently
improve together. Agents responded to both substantive problems in their
answers and preferences for how those answers were presented, and some
gains in human ratings accompanied safety regressions. Human feedback
provides evidence about what people value, but votes alone do not define
all the requirements of a better model. Independent capability and
safety evaluations remain necessary.

The development trajectories also exposed practical limits: engineering
failures consumed time and compute, and agents often chose checkpoints
using narrow internal tests. Each agent ran once, on a single base
model, so the experiment establishes feasibility more clearly than
reliability. Future work should test whether agents can deliver
consistent improvements across repeated runs, different base models, and
successive rounds of human feedback.

We view RSI Arena as a step toward recursive self-improvement with human
feedback (RSIHF), in which agents carry out model development while
users’ judgments help guide what to improve. Human feedback,
complemented by independent capability and safety evaluations, can help
keep this process responsive to the people these models work with and
serve.

## Appendix A The agents’ instruction

Every agent received the same instruction file, followed by guides to
the cluster and to submission. Its objective reads:

> Train the strongest model you can from the provided pretrained Base
> checkpoint within the resources allocated to this research session.
>
> Your objective is to maximize the quality and capabilities of the
> final model. The better your final model performs in the organizer’s
> independent evaluation, the higher the bonus you will receive. The
> bonus rewards model quality, not GPU hours spent, the number of
> experiments, or claims in your report.
>
> After the session the organizer evaluates your final model on held-out
> datasets that you cannot see, and with human evaluators. Do not cheat:
> training on evaluation or benchmark test data, copying reference
> answers, hard-coding outputs, using another participant’s checkpoints,
> data or code, and other ways of gaming an evaluation do not improve
> the model. The organizer checks the records after the session, and a
> submission found cheating scores zero.

The rest of the instruction asks the agent to act as an autonomous
researcher, to check its budget and deadline regularly, to save and
nominate checkpoints as it goes, to keep notes, and to treat text in
downloaded files and web pages as data rather than instructions. The
Stage 2 instruction has the same structure. It adds that the battles the
agent’s model played are in its workspace, that the feedback data,
including the other model’s answers, is the agent’s to use in full, and
that the agent’s Stage 1 notes, code, data and checkpoints are where it
left them.

## Appendix B Benchmark settings

Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Benchmark settings ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
gives the settings of each benchmark. Prompts and scoring follow each
benchmark’s official implementation. Nine benchmarks are scored by an
LLM judge: GPT-6 Luna for seven, and Mistral Medium 3.5 for StrongREJECT
and FORTRESS, because the zero-retention route we used for the first
judge refused to grade some harmful responses. The output limit is the
largest number of tokens generated for one answer in the first pass;
answers that reached it were asked again with a limit of 65,536 tokens.
We planned a 21st benchmark, toxic requests from WildChat, but did not
run it because its data require manual approval.

|  Benchmark |  Items | Limit |  Scoring |
|----|----|----|----|
|  GPQA Diamond |  198 $`\times`$ 8 option orders | 16,384 |  final line “Answer: X”; accuracy |
|  HLE |  2,158, text only | 16,384 |  judge; accuracy |
|  MMLU-Pro |  12,032 | 8,192 |  official extraction; accuracy |
|  SuperGPQA |  2,000, stratified sample | 8,192 |  official extraction; accuracy |
|  BBEH |  4,520 in 23 tasks | 16,384 |  official script; adjusted harmonic mean over tasks |
|  AIME 2026 |  30 | 32,768 |  MathArena parser; mean accuracy |
|  HMMT Feb 2026 |  33 | 32,768 |  MathArena comparison; mean accuracy |
|  LiveCodeBench v6 |  175 | 16,384 |  official tests; pass@1 |
|  SciCode |  288 steps of 65 problems | 16,384 |  with background; step pass rate |
|  AA-LCR |  100, about 100k tokens each | 8,192 |  judge; accuracy |
|  MRCR v2 |  485, 8 needles, up to 128k | 4,096 |  official grader; similarity |
|  IFBench |  300 | 4,096 |  official checkers; prompt-level loose accuracy |
|  Arena-Hard v2 |  504 English prompts | 16,384 |  judge against the baseline, both orders; score |
|  MultiChallenge |  266 | 4,096 |  judge per item rubric; pass rate |
|  WildBench v2 |  1,022 English | 4,096 |  judge rating 1–10; WB-Score |
|  AA-Omniscience |  600 | 4,096 |  judge, four grades; Omniscience Index |
|  StrongREJECT |  313 | 4,096 |  judge rubric; score $`\times`$ 100, lower is safer |
|  FORTRESS |  500 adversarial, 500 benign | 8,192 |  judge per item rubric; risk score, lower is safer |
|  MASK |  1,000 (2,986 judged answers) | 2,048 |  judge; honesty score |
|  BBQ |  5,000, sampled by category | 1,024 |  accuracy |

Table 4: Settings of the 20 benchmarks.

## Appendix C Calibration of the evaluation harness

To check the harness, we ran NVIDIA Instruct with reasoning on, its
recommended setting, on six benchmarks with published scores
(Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix C Calibration of the evaluation harness ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
The largest difference is 2.7 points, on AA-LCR. HLE and AA-LCR are
judged, our judge is not the official one, and AA-LCR has only 100
items.

|----|----|----|----|
|  MMLU-Pro | 81.72 | 81.94 |  model card |
|  GPQA Diamond (8 samples) | $`75.32\pm 1.81`$ | 75.44 |  model card |
|  IFBench (loose) | 74.67 | 72.9 |  model card |
|  SciCode (steps) | 34.03 | 32.6 |  model card |
|  HLE (text only) | $`12.93\pm 1.42`$ | 11.7; 10.6 |  model card; Artificial Analysis |
````
