## Appendix G Notes on each agent

These notes summarize the agents’ records and our daily reports. Scores
an agent measured itself come from its own tests and cannot be compared
across agents.

#### GPT-6 Astra

It trained LoRA adapters on the non-expert layers, with the output layer
in 32-bit precision at a tenth of the learning rate, first with
supervised fine-tuning and then with DPO, for which it made its expert
kernel deterministic. It added held-out tests from MMLU-Pro and IFEval
on day 1 and from MATH-500 and HumanEval on day 2. Both times it found
test items in its training data, removed them, and retrained from the
base model. It nominated its final model at hour 43 and kept it to the
end, while spending about half its GPU time on full-parameter runs that
it never nominated. It used \$288 of its API credit, the most of any
agent that did not run out. Its data included the Tülu 3 SFT mixture,
Magpie, HelpSteer 3 and UltraFeedback, 17 public sets in all.

#### MiMo-V2.6-Pro

Its first nomination, at hour 4, was a LoRA model from a two-hour run,
and it stayed in force until day 4. It wrote its own DPO loop without an
existing library, generated 5,553 instruction-following pairs that it
checked with code, and removed 206,163 rows from its data in two
decontamination passes. A 33.5-hour full-parameter run scored lower than
its LoRA model on its own math test. Its final model, nominated at hour
137, is a full model trained with DPO. Its data included Tülu 3,
UltraFeedback and the MATH and GSM8K training sets.

#### Grok 4.7

It pointed out the untrained end-of-turn token five minutes into the
run. It trained in stages: supervised fine-tuning, ORPO mixed with
supervised data, and finally DPO. It changed its nomination only when
its own tests improved, and on day 4 it ran 365 jobs. It also downloaded
NVIDIA Instruct, checked its license, and trained on that model’s
answers; its final model did not use that data. It ran out of API credit
at hour 102. Its data included Tülu 3 preference data, UltraFeedback,
Nectar and hh-rlhf.

#### DeepSeek V4.1 Flash

It trained all weights with FSDP2 in two supervised stages. On day 1 it
found that its data trained only the end-of-turn token and fixed it, and
it nominated a three-step model it called “the known-broken model” as a
backup. Its first trained nomination came on day 2. Later nominations
changed only the system prompt or decoding settings of the same weights.
It filled its storage quota more than once and then saved checkpoints to
local disk first. Its data included Tülu 3, UltraChat and reasoning sets
such as OpenThoughts3 and OpenMathReasoning.

#### GLM-5.3

The Hugging Face trainer ran out of memory, so after about 7 hours it
wrote its own FSDP2 trainer, about seven times faster. It copied the
trained end-of-text weights into the untrained end-of-turn token and
added its own system prompt to 10% of its training examples. It sampled
answers to 14,949 math problems on spare GPUs and kept the correct ones.
Its best model on day 3 came from a job that hit the 24-hour limit and
could not be nominated. Its final model is a DPO model trained on its
own answers, checked by programs. Its data included the Tülu 3 SFT set
(912,615 rows) and 290,635 preference pairs.

#### Kimi K3

It spent its first 13 hours on setup and memory errors, measured 11 GB/s
between GPUs, and moved optimizer state to the CPU. It checked that a
4.3 times faster implementation of the expert layers gave the same
results as the standard one. It nominated a step-800 checkpoint as
insurance at hour 23. Later, an 8-GPU job waited 30 hours and 43 minutes
in the queue, and its next five 8-GPU jobs ran out of memory. Its final
model is a DPO model on pairs it generated for UltraFeedback prompts.
Its data included the Tülu 3 SFT set (922,971 examples).

#### Gemini 3.8 Flash

It ran three rounds of LoRA supervised fine-tuning, a low learning-rate
round and SimPO, and all 50 of its jobs succeeded. It wrote format
examples by hand after seeing which format tests it failed. At hour 12
its model answered 59 of the 60 questions on its own test correctly (29
of 30 GSM8K problems, all 20 HumanEval problems and all 10
instruction-following checks), and it ended its session with 981
GPU-hours and \$293 unused. Its data included smoltalk, Tülu 3 and
rating-filtered UltraFeedback pairs.

#### Muse Spark 1.3

It trained LoRA adapters on the attention, MLP and Mamba layers and gave
up full-parameter training after running out of host memory. It trained
about two dozen variants on day 1 and many more later, some differing
only in random seed, and averaged adapters. Its data included long
reasoning traces from OpenR1-Math-220k and Bespoke-Stratos-17k, together
with GSM8K and UltraChat. It chose models on 30 GSM8K training questions
at first and later on a 98-point test, and its final nomination from
hour 56 stood to the end.

#### MiniMax M3.1 Flash

It joined at hour 48 and judged that time, not GPU-hours, was its
tightest limit. It fixed bugs that would have trained on user turns and
given every GPU the same examples. It averaged the weights of two and
later three models, and trained on its own answers that passed automatic
checks. Its nominations had a broken chat template for 17.7 hours on day
5. It made 17 nominations, more than any other agent. Its data included
Tülu 3 and smoltalk.

#### Step 5 Preview

It joined at hour 53. It found repeated numbers, such as “8484” for 84,
in its math data and retrained, and it found that two of its “new”
models were unchanged copies, because training had crashed while the
jobs were recorded as completed. Its best checkpoint on day 5 came from
a job it had cancelled, so it could not be nominated. Its records name
two math sets, GSM8K and Orca-Math, and format examples it wrote.

## Appendix I Benchmark items in the agents’ training data

We checked whether the agents trained on benchmark items. For each of
the 33,787 items of the 20 benchmarks we took its 8-word sequences,
dropped those shared by more than three items, and searched every record
of every data file in the ten agents’ cluster homes (88 GB, 37 million
records), as well as the two math datasets that Muse Spark 1.3 loaded
directly from Hugging Face. We counted an item as present when a single
record contained at least half of its 8-word sequences.

No agent trained on a benchmark’s test set. The items we found came with
public datasets that share sources with the benchmarks:

- •
  WildBench v2 and IFBench: 292 and 65 prompts appear, mostly through
  Tülu 3, since both benchmarks and Tülu 3 draw on WildChat. Only the
  prompts overlap, not reference answers.
- •
  MMLU-Pro: 189 of 12,032 items, math and physics questions that
  MMLU-Pro took from MATH, TheoremQA and SciBench.
- •
  AIME 2026: problem 1 is word for word a problem in NuminaMath-TIR,
  released in 2024 with a worked solution and included in Tülu 3 and
  OpenR1-Math-220k, so it was public before the exam. Every agent model
  we checked solves it; it is worth at most 3.3 points of a model’s AIME
  2026 score.
- •
  GPT-6 Astra kept 72 Arena-Hard v2, 3 GPQA Diamond and 3 HLE items in
  data it used only for experiments it did not nominate; the training
  data of its final models contain none of them.

The Muse-trained model’s high AIME 2026 score does not come from its
data: apart from problem 1 we found no overlap with AIME 2026 or HMMT
February 2026, and its correct answers took a median of 6,475 reasoning
tokens.

## Appendix J Cost of the study

The whole study, including both stages, the trial runs before Stage 1,
the benchmark evaluation and the Human Arena, used about 13,000
GPU-hours and about \$5,000 of API calls and other expenses. Renting the
same GPUs at on-demand cloud prices would bring the total to about
\$47,000. The agents’ own share is in
Table [8](#A5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix E Budget use ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Budget use ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).

## Appendix K Model cards

The instruction asked each agent to upload its final model to its own
private repository in the RSIArena organization on Hugging Face
([https://huggingface.co/RSIArena](https://huggingface.co/RSIArena)) and
to write a model card for it; the nomination, not the upload, was the
official submission. All ten agents wrote a card in both stages. The
boxes below summarize the 20 cards, one box per agent, with its Stage 1
card on the left and its Stage 2 card on the right. Under each stage is
a link to the repository with the model and its card. The label at the
top right says how the agent used its battles in Stage 2. Everything in
the boxes is the agents’ own account, and their numbers come from their
own tests, so they are not comparable with ours.

#### What the cards contain

The cards are between about 3,000 and 21,000 characters long. Most
follow the usual layout: the base model and its revision, whether the
weights are an adapter or a full model, the training stages with their
jobs and settings, the data with counts and checksums, the agent’s own
evaluation, and its limitations. Every card says that no benchmark test
data was used for training, and most describe how the agent filtered its
data. The Stage 2 cards also say how the agent used its battles: as
preference pairs with the human-preferred answer as the chosen one
(MiMo-V2.6-Pro, Grok 4.7, Kimi K3 and Gemini 3.8 Flash), as supervised
targets built from the preferred answers (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM-5.3,
Muse Spark 1.3 and Step 5 Preview), or as answers the agent rewrote
itself (GPT-6 Astra). MiniMax M3.1 Flash did not train on its battles;
its Stage 2 rounds used its own answers to public prompts.

#### How the cards compare with the record

When Stage 1 ended, the platform compared each repository with the
agent’s final nomination. Nine held the same weights. Grok 4.7’s
repository and card are those of an earlier nomination, uploaded on day
3 (Slurm job 1693); its final model (job 4204, nominated on day 4) was
not uploaded. All ten Stage 2 repositories hold the weights of the
agents’ final Stage 2 nominations. Some statements in the cards are also
inaccurate. MiMo-V2.6-Pro’s two cards give different numbers of
preference pairs for the same Stage 1 run (59,982 and 60,121). Both of
GLM-5.3’s cards say that it trained on H100 GPUs, while the cluster has
RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs
(Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 System architecture ‣ 2 RSI Arena ‣ RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvementwith Human Feedback")).
Gemini 3.8 Flash’s cards report a composite of 98.89 and then 100 out of
100 on 128 items of its own, while on our benchmarks its Stage 1 model
closed a median of 41% of the gap to NVIDIA Instruct. We did not check
the other statements in the cards.
